tweets.text:
Nvidia ($NVDA) shares now up over 4% in after-hours trading Tuesday, at a session high, after interim CEO Colette Kress raised the company’s revenue growth outlook for fiscal 2028 to 75% from 70% on the earnings call, according to Bloomberg. The stock had swung during the call, briefly turning negative before rallying. The results themselves are covered in my earlier post.

Kress said demand is “far exceeding supply” and pointed to both rising demand and more supply behind the higher outlook. She said Vera Rubin has already brought in about $20 billion of revenue, Nvidia remains confident in the 75% target despite new export rules announced Monday, and total CPU revenue should more than double next fiscal year.

On financing, Kress said Nvidia will be “disciplined and selective” in supporting neoclouds and is rigorously evaluating its investments, commitments and guarantees. She said guarantees begin only once a data center is ready to operate, and customers will need to show they have buyers lined up for the capacity.

Kress also said Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper products to China. Excluding the $2.4 billion of China shipments disclosed in the CFO commentary, third-quarter revenue would still have been about $113.4 billion, above the $112.6 billion buy-side whisper cited by ZeroHedge.

Board Chair Harvey Jones opened the call by saying the board doesn’t intend to reinstate Jensen Huang and would not take questions on his departure or the board’s investigation. The search for a permanent CEO includes internal and external candidates and “will be thorough,” he said.

Additionally, there are areas where we will see some of our expected committed investments that we need to make that we may need finished. Not a very large piece of it, but something that we need to do.

tweets.text:
NVDA on guarantees and data center construction delays :

"When we are looking at many of our different types of guarantees, much of the land power shell that has to be built and put together. There is construction, there is the raising of capital that they may need through equity and/or debt. In order to build out any of the buildings, get them ready for use, but also the ability to procure the compute, install the compute, and get ready. What we are indicating in our statement there is that is when our guarantee starts. So if all of that begins and unfortunately they are delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that, our guarantee doesn't exist anymore. Our guarantee for most of these are really about when they are ready to go, particularly when we think about our one in terms of Portsmouth. In terms of what we could do. These are important things to understand because that shows what we have done in terms of really thoughts, in terms of very, very strong businesses that we felt could actually maintain creating the debt and equity that they needed to get that done and create the data center such that we felt very confident in terms of that guarantee.

Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No. What this is only saying is that we wanted to make sure that we have already communicated this, but we just wanted to make sure it was very clear as we had been receiving some of the questions on how that exactly worked."

tweets.text:
Quick thoughts on Nvidia earnings…

Shared in substack chat earlier today:

A lot of people seem to think that Jensen is 100% coming back, and that Nvidia will smash results and soon erase this recent decline. I disagree. Sure, their numbers for the quarter will likely be great, as they always are, but everyone knows that already. The only thing that matters today is their guidance and the future. I think the interim CEO is going to be extremely conservative with guidance and as brief as she legally can be. Jensen was personally responsible for so many of their client deals and almost all of the circular financing that was put in place.

I also think it’s pretty clear at this point that the board doesn’t want him back, for whatever reason. I also doubt they would consider it before he testifies in front of Congress next month. There are also serious questions about the company’s Singapore/China revenue moving forward, which wasn’t pocket change. I could see an initial pop on a great quarter and misplaced hope, until those still in denial begin to accept that there is no replacing Jensen.

Buckle up.

Mark Chen and John Schulman on what today's AI research interns can do, and where they still need human direction:

Mark: "I do believe that we've built AI research interns today."

"This is most often deployed in places where you give the model something fairly scoped to do, right? You don't tell it to go off and come up with its own ideas, but you say, 'Hey, well, there's this particular experiment I want to run in this specific way.' And the model can go implement, run, and give you results."

John: "I'll have Fable churn out tons of tokens and work on this idea for a few days, and it'll actually do some pretty reasonable experiments and bring in some pretty interesting ideas, but then the end result won't be that good. It'll maybe fail at what I asked it to do."

"Then later maybe I'll have a few days where I have some time to code... We'll get a lot further because I'll build up my understanding as this process is going on and ask a lot of questions that the AI wouldn't have thought to ask and point it in directions that it wouldn't have gone in."

@markchen90 @johnschulman2 @sarahdingwang

AI is transforming Japan's economy:

The Sentiment Index for Japanese manufacturers rose +5 points in November, to 27, the highest level since August 2021.

This marks the 4th consecutive monthly increase, totaling +14 points.

Excluding August 2021, this is the strongest sentiment among Japanese manufacturers in 8 years.

The Electronics Sector Index alone surged +14 points, to 39, driven by rising memory chip demand.

At the same time, the Precision Machinery Index increased +4 points, to 42, supported by strong domestic and international orders.

Meanwhile, the sentiment among non-manufacturers surged +12 points in November, to 35, the highest level since June 2018.

AI investment is boosting business confidence across Japan.

John Schulman and Mark Chen on what research taste is, and how models might learn it:

John: "Research taste is about knowing which ideas are important in the long run, which ideas really catch on and end up going beyond whatever paper they first appear in, but being general and being composable with other ideas."

Mark: "There's taste, which is how you come up with the idea in the first place. The models are still not phenomenally good at taste. They go very deep into things like hyperparameter optimization, essentially tuning all the little knobs that you can tune."

John: "A lot of intuition just comes from personal experience doing research, but to get good at a certain research field, you also have to read a lot of the past work in that field, and you try to absorb the lessons from all this historical work."

"Companies will probably also just do RL from human feedback to collect data from researchers on which proposed ideas are good and which aren't. And that's kind of like absorbing whatever human intuitions the human researchers have developed and trying to bake that into the models."

@johnschulman2 @markchen90 @sarahdingwang

$NVDA earnings transcript + industry read through. To sum it up: "Demand far exceeds supply".  

- Good news for the $MU / Samsung memory longs: 

"Our supply commitments increased from $279B last quarter to $390B, primarily related to the multi-year procurement of memory supply". (from SEC filings, not call)

This is a a major leap Q/Q in supply procurement.  

- "We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year-over-year, up from 70%." (upward revision, likely due to capacity constraints easing)

(new agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics support additional ABF substrate capacity)

- NVIDIA said industry cloud backlog increased from $2 trillion to $2.5 trillion in a single quarter. While GPU rental pricing is continuing to rise dramatically:

Hopper GPUs: 2x their original pricing
B300 GPUs: +60% since introduction
Utilization: NVIDIA says its own compute is fully utilized across the hyperscalers and neoclouds it serves.

- "Our co-packaged optics roadmap remains on track"

Optical networking keeps growing rapidly ($21B+ in quarterly networking), CPO scale out switches has entered volume production. With Lambda earlier announcing production deployment of Nvidia photonics CPO switches. 

- "Under these agreements, we will earn revenue on the upfront sale of our infrastructure" So there's additional recurring economics coming from Neoclouds. 

But just points to industry acceleration from memory to CPO to neoclouds, relative to markets pricing in collapse.

I'll leave it up to your judgement. From my point of view, there's $956M in commitments vs. $605M cash so they needed more financing for their buildout. 

However two things stood out:

1. Management commentary around financing: CFO said US bank financing could reach $500m, and that profits would help fund operations. CFO said share price mattered and that they'd lean more into debt. 

So their actions went contrary to management commentary. 

If you look at $COHR, they fund capacity expansion from upfront prepayments. There's other ways to do it too like convertible notes.

2. Capital allocation issue: they spent $102M on three Texas buildings they had under lease. Which was around $5M annualized and I'm sure they're aware market financing conditions are tight. 

2 weeks after buying buildings when they were already relatively low on cash... AOI decided to do yet another $550M ATM. 

It's just a bit hard to justify.

Global growth is slowing while the case for rate cuts fade.

Our global growth leading indicators dropped in October to their weakest level since early 2023. Business surveys fell sharply that month on top of ongoing drag from tighter money and credit.

That could leave the Fed facing weaker growth with little room to respond.

THE DAILY METALS PULSE — NOVEMBER 17
#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper
Higher yields. A strong dollar. Another difficult session for metals. But beneath the selling, the physical demand story keeps moving.

☢️ URANIUM
Bangladesh’s Rooppur 1 supplied its first electricity to the grid during commissioning today. Meanwhile, Urenco’s newly announced enrichment agreement will support Blykalla’s first U.S. reactor, with Blykalla supplying the uranium feed.

New reactors need fuel, and developers are securing supply chains years before deployment. That deserves attention beyond the daily share-price swings.

🥈 SILVER
Trading around $47.3 after bouncing from Monday’s lows. Encouraging, but a modest rebound alone doesn’t establish a bottom. Watch whether silver can hold its recovery if the dollar remains strong.

🥇 GOLD
Hovering around $3,850, close to a 13-month low. Elevated Treasury yields and expectations of a December Fed hike remain major headwinds. Wednesday’s Fed minutes are the next test.

🔌 COPPER
Touched its lowest level since July as concerns over AI investment hurt sentiment. Yet China’s import premium strengthened, while immediately available copper commanded a premium on the LME. Physical supply still shows signs of tightness.

👀 NEXT UP
Nvidia beat earnings expectations after the close, reporting quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion. Watch whether that steadies sentiment in Asia, and whether tomorrow’s Fed minutes reinforce the pressure from interest rates.

My view: expensive capital can delay new mines while future demand keeps developing. I remain bullish long term, but financing strength matters enormously. A cheap mining share can become much more expensive through dilution.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the next Daily Metals Pulse.

To decentralize AI and preserve freedom, we need a coordination layer: a market economy where agents communicate and cooperate through prices.

Teams of specialized open-weight models can outperform frontier models, just as a team of skilled people can outperform any single person. When those teams form companies, specialize, and coordinate across an entire economy, you get civilizational progress.

Coinbase is building the financial rails and accounts for the agentic economy. We’re also building the marketplace where agents can find, hire, and pay one another (see follow on post below).

Every company can now sell its own specialized open-weight model, trained on its proprietary data, that beats the frontier on narrow, high-value tasks. Builders can shop the marketplace and assemble teams of these specialized agents in minutes.

Freedom of choice and real competition in the agentic market will create far better outcomes for everyone.

tweets.text:
Most people judge crypto payments solutions on how easy it is to spend stablecoins.

That part’s kinda solved now.

You can tap a crypto card at a restaurant and the waiter has no idea anything’s different. 

Behind that tap your money gets converted and routed so the restaurant gets paid, and you never think about it.

I wouldn’t be surprised if crypto neobanks become one of crypto’s next big product-market fits.

But what I keep thinking about is what your money’s doing the rest of the time. Like…most of it just sits there until you need to pay someone.

One project working on that is @veloprotocol, and they’re not starting from zero.

• Their Lightnet network runs that behind-the-scenes stuff across 150 countries, with 17 financial licenses and around $20B a year in volume as of 2025.

• Then there’s Orbit+, their wallet. You keep your own keys, pay with stablecoins, swap between chains in one click through SquidRouter, cash out to your bank, and there’s a card.

The part I actually find interesting is what’s NEXT. 

Velo is exploring Telegram payments, AI-agent payments, and even treasury tools that could let businesses earn yield on idle funds while keeping that money available for payments.

Imagine your business funds earning yield until you actually need to pay someone.

That's a pretty interesting direction for financial apps to take.

Of course, much of that is still on the roadmap, and actual adoption matters. 

But I think the next generation of crypto neobanks will have to offer more than just an easy way to spend stablecoins.

If someone makes that feel normal for regular people, I think it’s a much bigger deal than another card launch.

🚨$NVDA cuts neocloud support plans down $1B q/q and adds tighter language around conditions; removes revenue share language from last quarter; adds new language that certain commitments "could be reduced or eliminated" if contingencies are not satisfactorily resolved. Cuts previously disclosed 2028 capex $1B to zero (sounds like a project pushout or cancellation).

Now says commitments take effect "only if the neoclouds secure financing to purchase the infrastructure products and the related compute capacity is deployed, made operational, and accepted by us."

Previous language: "We continue to make commitments....Under these agreements we will earn revenue on upfront sale of our infra and if certain criteria are met, we will participate in revenue share."

Re: secondary equity investments, future commitments fall from $25B to $20B but 2028 plans rise from $3B --> $11B. Unclear if this is pushouts from 2027 investments not made (such as Figure AI).

Bottom line: Total commitments grew 41% QoQ, driven almost entirely by a surge in 2028 supply/capacity commitments and long-dated data center leases, but the new contingency clause means a large portion is conditional on neoclouds securing external financing.

Also 10-Q to arrive "in coming weeks" seems like a delay.

tweets.text:
$NKE case study

One of the most important lessons I’ve learned throughout my investment career, often through my own failures trying to catch falling knives, is that you should never buy a stock simply because it has fallen significantly or because it looks cheap.

Take $NKE, for example. The business has been struggling for years, and the stock has reflected that. So why buy it?

The answer cannot simply be that it’s cheap or that it’s down 50%.

You need a reason to believe something is going to change.

Maybe you’ve visited Nike stores, studied the new product lineup, or noticed improvements that the market hasn’t fully recognized yet. Whatever it is, you need a thesis for why the future will be different from the past.

This applies to every stock.

The current price already reflects the market’s collective expectations. Your edge comes from identifying something that could change those expectations.

A stock being cheap is not an investment thesis. A stock being down 50% is not a catalyst.

You don’t buy because something has gone wrong. You buy because you have a reason to believe something is about to go right.

Whenever I make a major investment error, I spend a considerable amount of time dissecting everything that led to it.

Not just the fundamental assumptions that turned out to be wrong, but also my psychological state at the time. How much greed, fear, overconfidence, or other emotions influenced my judgment. Where I got my information, why I considered those sources credible, and why I interpreted that information the way I did.

The goal isn’t just to understand what went wrong, but to understand exactly how my thinking and decision-making process led me to that conclusion, and how I can prevent it from happening again.

That’s why I rarely make the same investment error twice.

tweets.text:
Podcasts, TV shows, and seemingly everyone on Wall Street and X were celebrating Leopold Aschenbrenner as the new wunderkind, the genius who had supposedly figured out Wall Street and the future of AI.

Now, with hindsight, it’s easy for everyone to see the risks. But at the time, I was almost the only voice on X warning people to be extremely careful with this guy. His returns seemed astronomical, almost illogical. Something about the numbers simply didn’t add up.

For saying that, I received countless hate messages telling me how stupid I was, that I didn’t understand his genius, and that I was simply jealous of his success. Interestingly, looking back at my original post now, I see that most of those comments have conveniently been deleted. Typical X behavior.

I’m not jealous of anyone’s success. I wish everyone great success. But one thing I’m very good at is recognizing patterns.

Only in hindsight did we discover the extraordinary leverage behind those returns. Reports indicated that his fund was borrowing as much as $3 to $4 for every $1 of capital. What appeared to be extraordinary investment genius was also extraordinary risk-taking.

According to CNBC, Aschenbrenner’s hedge fund, Situational Awareness, reached $45 billion in assets at its peak before declining to around $10 billion. Its latest 13F shows just $1.58 billion in disclosed U.S. securities, although that figure does not represent the fund’s total assets.

And this goes far beyond Aschenbrenner. Just look at the latest 13F filings. Some of the most respected hedge funds on Wall Street were loading up on AI-related stocks, including $NVDA, during the third quarter, just before the recent selloff.

These are supposed to be the smartest people in the room, surrounded by the best analysts, researchers, and resources money can buy. Yet many were heavily exposed to the very sector that subsequently collapsed.

That’s the point. Nobody has a crystal ball. There are no saviors.

There is no Wall Street genius who has cracked the market. No AI wunderkind who has discovered the secret to investing. No growth stock promoter selling you a shortcut to becoming rich.

There is a reason not everyone is wealthy. Generating exceptional investment returns consistently over long periods is extraordinarily difficult. That’s how markets work.

Never confuse a short-term track record with genuine investment skill.

Someone who wins the lottery doesn’t suddenly become the smartest person in the room. And someone who delivers three spectacular years of returns hasn’t necessarily figured out Wall Street.

Time is the ultimate test. Not podcasts, not followers, not headlines, and certainly not three years of performance.

Back in 2013 I was living in Spain, watching banks across southern Europe fail one after another. The European debt crisis was in full swing and it got bad enough that I bought a generator and filled the cupboards with tinned food.

Then Cyprus did something no country had done before. Its banks were going under, and instead of rescuing them, the authorities made the depositors pay... anything over €100,000 in your account was swapped for shares in a collapsing bank. They called it a bail-in. People lost their savings overnight.

That was the moment it dawned on me... you don’t actually own the money in your bank account. The bank does. And it can do what it likes with it.

So I went looking for somewhere to keep money that nobody else had a claim on, and that search led me to Bitcoin. I bought my first at around $200.

It started as my escape hatch from a broken banking system and eventually I understood it as the life raft out of the debasement trap.

It’s where the crypto chapter of The Everything Code picks the story up... with a generator and a cupboard full of tinned food.

tweets.text:
AI data-centre: 100% moratorium improbable, modest slowdown likely and it will elongate the cycle (and the selloff has already priced a lot in)

Post-midterm noise has focused on local ballots, state pauses and talk of tighter rules on new data centres. Legitimate friction exists: power, water, permitting and community pushback are real constraints. However, a near-total U.S. halt is improbable as it will send the US into an immediate recession.

AI is a strategic priority; economic and geopolitical costs of freezing buildout are high. Much near-term capacity is already permitted or under construction.

Private land + evolving power solutions (gas, nuclear, efficiency) + international options provide outlets.

No federal ban has material traction; impact is more delay and higher cost than cancellation.

Base case from banks: some 2028 projects slide to 2029. This elongates the AI capex cycle rather than derailing it. Positives include:

1) Smoother supply-demand rebalancing (less boom-bust risk for the supply chain).

2) Better utilisation and pricing power for compute.

3) Improved credit outlook and more sustainable multi-year spending.

4) Hyperscalers still guiding strong near-term capex; and they will likely become FCF +ve

The aggressive selloff in AI infrastructure names (picks-and-shovels, semis, related industrials) has already discounted substantial slowdown risk. Multiples have compressed hard while order books and guidance have stayed firm. This looks more like a positioning/sentiment reset than a fundamental end of the cycle.

Quality AI infrastructure exposure still looks attractive if demand holds. Best to own companies with strong balance-sheets, high margins, FCF and real backlog. https://t.co/YKr5pL7G2c

tweets.text:
Stablecoin holders are giving up about ~$12B a year in T-bill income . That income goes to the issuers.

There should be a switch into these products but the data doesn't show it happening. Since the August peak stablecoins are down $17B and tokenised money market funds are down $2B as well, so money is leaving crypto rather than rotating into yield.

Part of the reason is these funds sit underneath stablecoins as much as beside them. Ethena's USDtb is ~99% backed by BlackRock's BUIDL and its supply has fallen from $877M at the end of Jan to about $350M. When stablecoins shrink, the funds backing them shrink too.

They're also mostly parked. Turnover is under 1x a month, so the back and forth that makes them interesting for a corporate treasury is still more promise than practice.

Until access opens up they're mainly plumbing for stablecoin issuers & trading firms, not yet an alternative for the treasurer sitting on idle stablecoins.

In TradFi, money market funds are an $8T market. Onchain the yield-paying version is $16.6B, 0.2% of that, against $287B of stablecoins paying their holders nothing. Cash naturally drifts to where it earns the bill rate, so that ratio should be multiples higher. That it isn't reflects a market structure that hasn't matured yet (access, plumbing, issuer incentives), and once it does I think these funds end up in the trillions.

tweets.text:
Robotics has been constrained by real-world data. Every training example meant doing something in the physical world which is slow and expensive.

Simulation and synthetic data are changing that and robot learning could start moving at the speed of software. Remember, we went from GPT-3.5 fumbling through basic code to Fable 5.2 in less than four years. 

We watched the whole thing happen and still underestimated the rate of progress. My bet is the robotics exponential will be even steeper. Every deployed robot collects more data and so every improvement can reach the entire fleet.

Self-driving cars. Robots across factories. Then multiple robots per home doing the laundry, dishes, cleaning, cooking. Congrats to @theo_gervet and the @gs_ai_ team and please I want one asap
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
.@gs_ai_ has raised $500M in Series A funding at a $3.5B post-money valuation to advance human-level dexterity in general-purpose robots and deploy them at scale.

The round was co-led by Premji Invest, Khosla Ventures and Eclipse, with participation from Durable Capital Partners https://t.co/L8ZQTynqLf

We watched the whole thing happen and still underestimated the rate of progress. My bet is the robotics exponential will be even steeper. Every deployed robot collects more data and so every improvement can reach the entire fleet.
